text: It's a planned disposal, not an accident. Cassini had little fuel left and its orbit was getting small, so the team ended the mission by diving it into Saturn. The real concern is the moons, especially Enceladus, with its subsurface ocean and plumes, and Titan, with its thick atmosphere and methane seas. If the spacecraft had just been left drifting, it could have wandered close to one of those bodies and dropped Earth microbes or organic molecules. Threading it into Saturn's atmosphere, where it burned up, keeps the probe away from places that might one day be explored for life.

I think it's mostly the stance and load. On a skateboard, the foot on the board has to keep the board level while the pushing leg is off the ground, so that 'stationary' leg ends up doing more balancing than you'd expect. It has to make tiny corrections with the ankle, knee, and hip, and even the core, especially if you're turning or going fast. If you're not used to it, those small stabilizing muscles get tired, and that can feel like a dull ache in the leg, knee, or hip.

I've seen this argued a lot, and the short version is that it isn't really 'stationary' in the way you mean. Your weight isn't just sitting there; it's being shifted and corrected all the time. If you ride with your back foot flat or too far back, or if your knees are locked, the leg has to compensate, and that often causes pain in the knee or lower back. I guess if you mostly hurt after a session, it's likely muscle fatigue; if it hurts during riding, it might be a positioning problem. Check that your feet are spaced about shoulder width, with your back foot angled a little, and that you keep a slight bend in your knees so your legs can absorb the little shocks and bumps.

Honestly, a lot of beginners make the mistake of trying to keep the stationary leg as still as possible, which makes the muscles tense up. Let it move slightly and use your whole body to balance. If the pain is sharp, in one spot, or comes with swelling or a clicking knee, then it's worth getting it looked at because that's different from ordinary soreness. And if you're new, give it a week or two and see if the ache fades.

I think the label’s about shared heritage, not a passport. Most U.S. Black people aren’t from Africa today, and I agree with that. But “Afro” refers to the African roots that came over with the transatlantic slave trade. So even if someone’s family’s been in America for generations, that history is part of the identity the name points to. It’s like calling people “Hispanic” when a lot of them aren’t from Spain either. The word “Afro” is meant to connect Black Americans to the broader continent, not to say every individual actually lives there. As far as I know, the term isn’t meant as a literal travel claim. I’ve seen this argument made a lot, and honestly it’s one of those naming things that trips people up. I guess it’s the same with “Anglo-American” for white Americans, even if most aren’t from England. So the mismatch feels unfair because the name evokes Africa as a whole, and that’s the main point people keep missing. It’s a historical link, not a current address.

As far as I know, most of the arms flow comes through Lebanon and Jordan, and there's a huge black market that runs across the borders. You get stuff from the Gulf states, some from the US, and a lot of it is just old stockpiles that have been sitting around for decades.

Why do they still get them? Well, the conflict hasn't really ended, and everyone knows that the one with the guns has the power. So even when things calm down a bit, the groups want to keep their options open. It's a classic security dilemma, really: if your neighbor is buying weapons, you feel you have to do the same.

Short version: the reason everyone thinks all drugs are bad is that the effect that makes them pleasurable is the same effect that makes your brain need more and more. I've seen this argued a lot, and honestly I think the "0 adverse effects" idea is a bit of a fantasy. Most recreational drugs work by flooding the brain's reward system, usually through dopamine, and that flood is what produces the high. But that same flooding changes how the brain expects rewards to work, so over time the normal stuff stops feeling as good. So the pleasure and the downside aren't two separate things you can tune independently; they're basically the same mechanism.

That's why tolerance and dependence show up. You need a bigger dose for the same hit, and your baseline mood and motivation can suffer. With something like heroics or stim-type drugs, the euphoric spike is intense, but it also pushes your nervous system into an extreme state, and that's where the adverse effects start: sleep disruption, cravings, mood swings, and the fear of withdrawal. I'd say the "no adverse effects" drug would have to give you the same dopamine surge without changing your brain's reward set-point, and I'm pretty sure that's almost contradictory. The pleasure you're asking for is exactly the thing that makes the brain adapt.

There are drugs that are milder, and some people argue that alcohol, nicotine or even certain supplements can be used carefully, but even those carry side effects if you push the dose. So I guess the honest answer is that no drug is truly free of costs. The brain is wired to treat intense, repeated pleasure as a signal, and that signal is what drives dependence. I've seen this pattern in my own life with a few substances, and the "I can stop whenever" phase always ends the same way. If a drug could give that intense euphoria with zero downsides, it would have to bypass the reward-adaptation loop, and I don't think any natural or synthetic drug actually does that.

Hi,

Yeah, that one confused me too. I think it's mostly the standing and walking, plus whatever stress or tension you're carrying into the day. A long shopping trip is a lot of low-grade physical strain, and if your shoes are bad or your feet get hot, it adds up. It's not "normal" because you're not doing anything intense, so your brain doesn't file it as exercise soreness. My back leg used to kill me when I started skating, but that was from pushing too hard too fast. For shopping, I'd check your shoes first and don't ignore the tension.

Take care,
Sam

Hi Sam,

That's a classic priming effect. Because you'd been repeating "silk" and spelling it out, the "ilk" bit was stuck in your head, and when he asked what cows drink, "milk" (same "ilk") was the first thing that came out. You weren't actually wrong about cows — the word milk was just the most activated in your working memory at that moment. Your brother wasn't quizzing you; he was showing how repetition hijacks your attention and pushes a related word to the front. It's the same kind of thing they use in memory tests, where repeating a word makes related words pop up. Honestly, you can even test it yourself: say "silk" five times, spell it, then ask a friend what cows drink. You'll see the same slip happen to you. So next time your brother does this, don't be embarrassed — it's literally how your attention works.

Talk soon,
Alex

Hi,

Yeah, house-buying is a mess if you don't plan it. First thing: get pre-approved for a mortgage before you start looking, because it stops you falling in love with a place you can't afford. Lenders will give you a rough figure and it makes you look serious to sellers.

Don't skimp on the deposit. In most places you'll need at least 10% down, and bigger deposits get you better rates. Then factor in stamp duty, legal fees and moving costs, because those sneaky extras can add thousands. Get quotes early.

I'd also push for a survey and a legal check before you commit. I've seen people sign before the lawyer found a big problem. And ask the seller for their disclosure: what's been repaired, any leaks, what's included in the price. If it's an older home, be especially careful with the roof, wiring and plumbing.

One more thing: don't race. The market feels urgent, but a bad deal is worse than missing a week. Take it slow, and ask your lender about fixed versus variable rates before you choose.

Cheers,
Your friend

Hi Anna,

Honestly, the short version is: it's a compromise, not a magic product. The difference is mainly formulation. A 3-in-1 has to work on both skin and hair, so it uses milder surfactants and more conditioning agents than a regular body wash or shampoo. That's why it feels softer and can rinse off hair without stripping it too much.

A 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner is aimed at hair only, so it can be more aggressive with cleansing and conditioning. The 3-in-1 has to stay mild enough for your whole body, which means it's a little weaker at getting hair fully clean if you have very dirty or product-heavy hair. For body, it's basically a body wash with extra conditioning ingredients, not a full replacement for a dedicated soap if you want a deeper clean.

I'd use it when I'm lazy or traveling; if my hair needed serious cleaning, I'd still reach for separate shampoo and conditioner. Also, I've noticed that some 3-in-1s are just rebranded 2-in-1s with a marketing label, so reading the ingredient list is the fastest way to tell if there's really a separate body-wash formula inside. I wouldn't expect it to outperform the separate products.

Talk soon,
Leo

Hey Sam,

I've seen this come up a few times, and the practical answer is geodetic GPS. What they do is set up GPS reference stations on top of each tectonic plate, then track the fixed points' movement relative to stations on neighboring plates over months or years. The hardware is basically the same tech as your phone, but mounted on tall poles anchored in bedrock so local building motion doesn't skew the readings. Once you have velocities for each plate, you can compare adjacent ones and get a rate for, say, North America and Eurasia drifting apart; the North Atlantic is widening while the Pacific is closing, so the rates vary a lot, but the principle is the same — just more precision and longer baselines. The speeds are tiny in daily terms — roughly 2 to 10 cm per year depending on the plate pair, with the fastest spreading ridges near the upper end — so you'll never notice it yourself, but that's millions of years of accumulation. Paleomagnetic stripes on the seafloor and fossil matches were the original clues that plates move at all; modern GPS is how we get the actual current velocity.

That's the short version.

Cheers,
Alex

Inbreeding makes offspring more likely to inherit two copies of the same rare recessive mutation, because relatives share more of the same ancestry. Many of these recessive alleles are mildly harmful and often affect brain development, so when they pair up, the child can show cognitive effects. It is not that inbreeding itself makes a person less intelligent; it increases the chance that hidden genetic variations, which usually stay silent, become expressed. Over generations, small populations tend to accumulate these harmful alleles, raising the family’s genetic load. Since intelligence is shaped by many genes, the exposed variations can lower measured IQ. If two relatives have children, the kids have a higher chance of being homozygous for harmful recessive traits. That is why inbred offspring often score lower on IQ tests. The link is real, but it’s a population-level effect, not a guarantee for any one child.

Short version: it’s not that arm injuries are objectively less painful, it’s mostly about what’s there and what isn’t. Your arm has plenty of muscle, fat, and bone, but far fewer critical structures than, say, your head, chest, or abdomen. A lot of the “hurt less” feeling also comes from expectations. Arm injuries are common, so people mentally braced for them, and that changes how pain is processed. There’s also the fact that the arm isn’t usually the first place you’d expect a bad wound, so a graze or a shallow cut can feel “mild” by comparison.

In my experience, the biggest difference is the contrast: getting hit in the arm doesn’t feel as alarming as a hit to the torso or neck, because those areas protect things that can fail fast. And pain is subjective, so if the arm is swollen or the bone is bruised, it will still hurt plenty.

Why CO is far more dangerous than CO2 to breathe down: the short version is that CO and oxygen compete for the same binding spot on hemoglobin, and CO wins by a wide margin. CO sticks to hemoglobin roughly 200 to 250 times more strongly than oxygen, so even a small amount crowds oxygen out of the blood, and because the binding reverses slowly, your tissues start starving for oxygen while you're still breathing normally.

That's the real difference with carbon dioxide. CO2 isn't a competitor for that hemoglobin spot in the same way; it's a normal waste product your body makes and exhales, so at everyday levels your lungs simply get rid of it. CO2 can still cause problems at high concentrations—it can make you dizzy or cause you to pass out if the air gets very concentrated—but it doesn't quietly block oxygen transport the way CO does.

What makes CO especially nasty is that you can't see, smell, or taste it, so you can be breathing it in while feeling totally fine until your head gets foggy or your chest feels tight. In places where you use fuel-burning equipment, I'd say treat any fuel-burning space as a CO risk and use a working CO alarm; it's the one check I never skip. A small leak in a furnace or garage can build up fast, and a person can be breathing CO without realizing for a while. That's why I always check the alarm battery and keep it in an open, ventilated spot. I mean, it's one of those things where the alarm is really the whole point, and if it beeps, clear the room, don't just ignore it.

In an aircraft emergency, the brace position is a protective posture you take when the flight attendant calls for it. It works by getting you into a compact, low-risk shape before impact.

The main idea is to reduce the chance of being thrown forward. You pull your knees in and bring your feet close together, bend forward, and press your hands against the seatback or the floor in front of you, keeping your head low and tucks toward your knees or chest. That reduces how far your body can lurch forward when the plane suddenly slows or hits something.

It also protects your head, neck, and torso. By tucking in and bracing, you limit the sudden jerks that can cause whiplash or head strikes. For people with back or neck issues, follow the guidance given to you, because the exact position may vary.

The brace position won't guarantee a safe outcome, but it does reduce the forces on your body. That's why you're asked to assume it during warnings or when told to brace.

Most of what we think of as businesses are products of the industrial era because large-scale manufacturing, distribution, and marketing only became possible after factories, railroads, and telegraph systems appeared. Before that, production was local and craft-based, so a workshop or trading post rarely grew into a name everyone knows. Records were patchy and there was little mass media, so older firms often vanished from memory. Industrialization also made it possible for companies to organize as large corporations, reach many customers, and build brand recognition across regions. That's why you see very few famous pre-industrial companies in modern business lists.

I bought my last car through a local bank after the dealership tried to sell me a lower rate that turned out to be less attractive than the bank’s deal. At first I didn’t get it either—how could the bank be the cheaper option when the dealer’s number was lower?

Here’s what I came to understand. Dealerships often advertise a lower interest rate, but that rate is usually tied to a specific manufacturer’s financing program and often comes with conditions. You might have to finance for a set term, keep the car for a minimum period, or use their service plan. Those strings can quietly make the total cost higher. A bank loan is more straightforward: you take the money, pay a fixed rate over a set term, and there’s usually less fine print around the loan itself.

The other big factor is fees. Dealer financing often includes a documentation fee, a “prepaid” servicing package, or a mandatory gap insurance add-on. Add those together and the effective cost climbs. When I compared my bank quote to the dealer’s package, the bank’s higher headline rate was offset by the smaller fee stack and by the fact that I wasn’t locked into dealer-specific terms.

There’s also the issue of negotiation. Dealers can quietly adjust the “low” rate or attach other charges unless you’re watching the numbers closely. A bank, by contrast, generally gives you a clear APR and a fixed payment. I found that the bank let me choose the term that fit my budget, and I could compare offers without a salesperson steering me.

One caveat: if you qualify for a subsidized manufacturer rate—say 0% or 1.9% on a new car—dealer financing can genuinely be cheaper. But those promos are rare, short-lived, and usually tied to new inventory. For used cars, or when no promo is available, the bank route tends to win on total cost because of the fee structure and flexibility.

The lesson I took away is that the advertised rate is only one line item. You have to add fees, mandatory add-ons, and restrictions before you can compare them. That’s why a bank can be the cheaper route even when the dealer’s sticker rate looks lower.

To me, marijuana's legality in US states is less about the plant and more about who gets to decide. I'm in favor of states being able to choose, but with some real limits. Medical use makes sense to me because it's not just a lifestyle choice for people with chronic pain or cancer-related nausea, and I've heard enough horror stories about insurance not covering it that state rules matter a lot. Recreational use is where I get really nervous. I think states should be able to allow it, but not flood the market without rules. I'd want taxes, age limits, and testing before it's sold. Honestly, the patchwork is pretty messy, but it also gives people somewhere to vote with their feet. That feels better than Washington DC deciding for everyone. If a state wants a pretty small, regulated market, let it, and let the others keep their rules too.

I keep getting asked how the body produces electricity, and I think the cleanest answer is: it's ion gradients, not little batteries. Cells pump sodium out and potassium in through protein pumps, so the inside sits around -70 mV relative to the outside. When a nerve fires, ion channels open, sodium rushes in, the charge flips, and that wave travels down the axon. That's the "spark" that makes your hand twitch or your heart beat. So the electricity is really just the movement of charged atoms through membranes, and it's what wires up your whole nervous system.

I've always found it weird that people get so mad about sampling. Like, I get that you're taking a recognizable bit of a song and putting it in yours, but honestly, that's what music has been doing for decades. You're not just grabbing a drum loop and calling it yours. You're cutting a few seconds out of a record, throwing it through an EQ, maybe pitching it down, time-stretching it, layering it under your own beats and vocals, and building something new around that fragment. It's collage. It's a conversation with the past.

The actual mechanics are pretty hands-on. Finding the source material is the easy part, whether that's an old vinyl, a CD, or a digital file. You load it into your DAW, mark in and out points, and pull out the exact two or three seconds you want. Then you process it, and that's the part people forget. You don't just drop a raw clip into the mix and hope for the best. It gets shaped. A low-pass filter makes it sound muffled and old. Boosting the highs makes a hi-hat stand out. Slowing it down, flipping it, or pitching it a few semitones turns the fragment into something recognizably related but no longer the same. That's the creative act. The clip is raw material, not a finished piece.

Licensing is where it gets messy, and I think people conflate the creative act with the legal one. If you're going to release a record commercially, you need to clear the sample. That means contacting the rights holders and either buying a sync license or negotiating a share. It can cost a lot, and sometimes the holder says no. But I don't think the legal hurdle makes the creative act less valid. You can make the music first and sort out the paper trail later, or you can build around what's already cleared.

The best sampling I've heard doesn't hide the source. It leans into the contrast. You can hear the old piano loop and the new hip-hop beat side by side, and the gap between them is where the interest lives. That's what I mean by conversation. It's not plagiarism if you're not pretending the fragment is yours. It's a reference, a nod, a piece of musical history being reused in a new context.

I think the fear of sampling comes from treating music as property instead of language. Language works by reusing words in new sentences. Music works the same way. You don't need permission from the inventor of the word love to use it. Same with a drum pattern from a 1969 record. You're not stealing, you're borrowing a building block.

I'll leave you with this: the most powerful thing I've seen in modern music is when the sample and the original track are so different that you hear the old song in the new one and the new song in the old one, and both feel right. That's when sampling stops being a trick and starts being a bridge.

I used to think headaches meant my brain was actually hurting, but now I mostly think of them as irritation of the pain-sensitive stuff around my head and neck. The brain itself is pretty much numb; what hurts is the tissue around it. For me, it usually kicks in when I’ve been hunched over a screen too long, or I’m dehydrated or haven’t slept. Then the muscles around my temples and neck get tight and start pulling, and that’s when the pressure builds. I’ve found that standing up, doing slow neck rolls, and drinking water helps take some of that tension off. It’s not always a warning of something terrible. Sometimes it’s just your body complaining that it needs rest or hydration.

Short version: absolute disaster. We got there at 7:20 p.m. Sunday, picked the place because we had a 10 p.m. show in the same hotel and figured it'd be easy. The food? Don't even know, we never got to eat. We put our names in their completely useless digital waitlist, got told to come back to pay at 8:23, did, then stood around till 8:40 before staff casually said we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15. Party of two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait's that far past payment, say it upfront so our night isn't completely wasted. Zero stars if that were an option.

Went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30, and I was genuinely surprised there wasn't a line. We came out to about $130 for two, which felt pretty steep. Going in, I figured the price would be roughly like a steakhouse, but after, I realized I actually paid a bit more than I thought I'd spend at one.

The thing that really bummed me was that there wasn't any steak. At that price I had assumed there'd be some steak option. The meat was lamb, prime rib, and chicken, and I get the feeling you can find those at other Vegas buffets for a lot less. The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. The legs are all over Vegas buffets, but I hadn't seen rock crab claws anywhere else, so that was pretty cool. The catch was there were no crab crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next one that I didn't want to smash shells and send bits at the people next to us. So I just stuck to the legs. The Asian station wasn't all that distinctive, and honestly it reminded me of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert was gelato and pastries, but nothing stood out. There were fresh juices too, though I didn't try any.

All in all I'd call it acceptable, but overpriced for what you get. If you're curious, I think it's worth trying once, especially if there's no wait. If the line is long though, I'd probably think twice.

The space bar rattles. Hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so example becomes eexample and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once in an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not even looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and now I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle.

I've been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life, well, the under-21 version of it, so I've sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly, it was mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

The circular stage is genuinely smart. You're looking down into it, so from nearly any seat you get a decent view, and that's rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too, the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not in a rip-off way exactly, just if you've seen Cirque, you've seen comparable feats with maybe more clarity.

Clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don't know. There's a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it's trying to say. Way too much happens at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many wow moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing, where more has to be better, so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you're staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal, $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn't pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn't blown away, and I don't think anyone else was either. A few friends liked it, and if you've never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don't expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years ago, I ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear over the telephone. They never arrived because the sales rep recorded the delivery address incorrectly. Her handwritten 7 was interpreted as 1. The intended address was 5407, but the package was sent to 5401. The folks at 5401 took it to the UPS store to return it, and it disappeared, and we never saw or heard from it again. We didn't learn until several weeks later. During the dispute, we placed an additional order for two more shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the original two. The owner handled it at that stage. He acknowledged the shipment went to the wrong address but said no refund unless the shirts were returned. He claimed we were partly responsible because we hadn't been friendly enough to the residents at 5401, four doors away. We disputed the original charge with our credit card company and eventually received a credit.
